newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Primakov and Solana start new NATO-Russia talks.
newsitem.headline: Primakov and Solana start new NATO-Russia talks.

text.p: Russian Foreign Secretary Yevgeny Primakov began talks with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Sunday on a NATO-Russia deal to run parallel with the alliance's eastwards expansion.
Both NATO and Moscow imposed a news blackout on the meeting, which Solana planned to conduct in a relaxed atmosphere over dinner after an hour of more formal talks.
Primakov gazed impassively out the window of his limousine as his motorcade sped past journalists into the secluded Brussels diplomatic street where Solana has his private residence.
The meeting, the second in five weeks between Primakov and Solana, was part of a frenzied round of diplomatic activity in which the West hopes to overcome Moscow's objections to NATO's enlargement.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin earlier renewed his attack on NATO's plans to give membership to some of Moscow's former satellites, but said he thought a compromise would be reached at a summit next month with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"We have agreed to look for a compromise and I think we will find this compromise at the summit we are holding with President Clinton on March 20-21 in Helsinki," he told reporters.

Yeltsin, who discussed the issue with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Moscow last week, said his country's aim was to stall enlargement for as long as possible and "not allow the renewal of confrontation."
His remarks appeared to confirm the view of several alliance diplomats who say that, despite Moscow's strident public rhetoric, they detected a wish by Russia to start real negotiations.

But Moscow's almost unanimous antipathy to NATO's expansion was clear when Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said the army was heading for financial ruin and the West might therefore try to place Russia's nuclear arsenal under United Nations control.
"NATO is making every effort to deprive Russia of its strategic nuclear forces," Rodionov was quoted as telling veterans.

NATO diplomats said that, after weeks of allied concessions from arms control to offers of close military cooperation, Solana planned to go on the offensive and try to get Primakov to offer something in return.

"Solana will push Primakov. What will Russia bring to a new relationship?" said one senior diplomat, adding that Solana would try to focus the discussions on the content of any final document rather than the exact form it should take.

Diplomats said the talks were likely to last around four hours. Primakov was due to leave early on Monday but his deputy Nikolai Afanasievsky would remain, possibly for detailed discussions with NATO Assistant Secretary-General Gebhard von Moltke.

Russia has made clear it wants a legally-binding treaty to govern its relations with NATO, while NATO prefers a more flexible political agreement which would not need ratifying by member states' parliaments.
Moscow says the final document should contain a commitment by the allies not to place troops and weapons on the territory of new members except for internationally-approved peace-keeping operations.
NATO, opposing any form of second-class membership, says it cannot accept outside conditions on where it positions its "infrastructure".
